speaker: John Schulman
title: John Schulman (OpenAI Cofounder) — Reasoning, RLHF, & plan for 2027 AGI
question: Why do post-trained AI chatbots from completely different labs end up converging on the same writing style and stylistic tics?
guest: I think there might be some funny effects going on where there's unintentional distillation happening between the language model providers. If you hire someone to go do a labeling task, they might just be pulling up their favorite chatbot, feeding the task in, having the model do the task, and then copy and pasting it back. So that might account for some of the convergence. But also, I think some of the things we're seeing are just what people like. I mean, I think people do like bullet points. They like the structured responses. People do often like the big info dumps that they get from the models. So it's not completely clear how much is just a quirk of the particular design choices of the post-training processes and how much is actually intrinsic to what people actually want.

points.core: Unintentional cross-lab distillation causes competing chatbots to share stylistic habits.
points.note: Accept: accidental model-to-model style contamination or cross-provider distillation leaking between labs' training pipelines. Do not credit: generic claims that all labs use the same transformer architecture or internet pretraining corpus.

points.core: Hired data labelers secretly paste outputs from rival chatbots into annotations.
points.note: Accept: contractors or annotators outsourcing labeling tasks to an existing chatbot and submitting copy-pasted completions as human data. Do not credit: deliberate synthetic data generation run by the lab itself.

points.core: Human evaluators genuinely prefer structured formatting like bulleted information dumps.
points.note: Accept: real user or rater preference for bullet points, clear structure, or comprehensive formatted answers rather than pure training artifacts. Do not credit: blaming only reward hacking or rater laziness without acknowledging genuine human preference for structure.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
Nobody has a fully settled answer, but the convergence most plausibly comes from shared pressures rather than coincidence.

The labs start from heavily overlapping pretraining data, then apply very similar post-training recipes. Each fine-tunes on demonstrations written to similar "helpful, clear, balanced" guidelines, often by the same pool of contract annotators, some of whom themselves use chatbots. They then optimize with RLHF against human raters who tend to reward the same surface features: confident structure, hedged balance, tidy summaries, enthusiastic politeness, and polished-sounding vocabulary.

Optimization also collapses diversity. Reward-driven fine-tuning pushes models toward a narrow, safe, high-probability register, so tics like "delve," rule-of-three lists, "it's not X, it's Y" contrasts and em dashes get amplified from mild human habits into signatures.

Finally, models contaminate each other. Labs train on synthetic data and distill from model outputs, benchmark against competitors, and scrape a web increasingly filled with chatbot text, so one model's quirks leak into the next generation.

The relative weight of these causes is still debated, and public evidence about annotator effects in particular is mostly circumstantial.

models.label: Gemini Carbon
models.answer: Post-trained chatbots converge stylistically because competing labs draw from a shared post-training ecosystem and optimize for identical incentives. First, major labs rely on the same handful of annotation vendors, whose human raters judge responses rapidly under similar rubrics for helpfulness, safety, and clarity. Under time pressure, raters consistently favor confident, diplomatic, structured prose, while shared rater demographics imprint distinctive lexical quirks like "delve" or "tapestry." Second, preference optimization methods like RLHF and DPO cause mode collapse: rather than preserving the messy diversity of pretraining text, models concentrate probability mass on safe, high-reward rhetorical templates, such as balanced hedging, em-dashes, and "it's not X, it's Y" contrasts. Finally, synthetic data and shared evaluations create a cross-lab feedback loop. Labs routinely train on synthetic outputs, overlapping preference datasets, and AI-contaminated web text, while using frontier models as automated judges and chasing public leaderboards like Chatbot Arena. Because automated judges and crowd benchmarks reward familiar assistant cadences, stylistic tics propagate across model families, locking independent architectures into one recognizable voice.

noweb.answer: Post-trained chatbots from rival labs converge on a distinct "AI voice" because they share overlapping human annotator pools, synthetic training data, and optimization pressures. During supervised fine-tuning and preference alignment, labs often hire the same third-party data vendors, whose contractors work under tight time limits and similar rubrics emphasizing helpfulness, neutrality, and safety. Raters skimming responses consistently reward well-structured, surface-fluent prose, favoring diplomatic hedging, neat transitions, and formal vocabulary like "delve" or "underscores"—choices often shaped by the regional English conventions of global annotator workforces. Reinforcement learning then amplifies these biases through mode collapse, narrowing a model's token distribution onto reliable, high-reward phrasing and rhetorical tics such as "it's not just X, it's Y." Crucially, synthetic cross-pollination cements this homogenization: labs routinely use existing frontier models to generate fine-tuning data and act as automated reward judges, while also ingesting web text and public datasets saturated with AI outputs. Optimizing against the same human heuristics and distilled model preferences ultimately drives independent architectures into a single, risk-averse stylistic equilibrium.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
They converge mainly because they're trained on overlapping data and optimized toward the same narrow target.

Pretraining gives every model roughly the same internet. That corpus now includes a lot of AI-generated text, so each new model partly learns the style of earlier chatbots. Post-training then narrows things further. Labs use similar recipes: supervised fine-tuning on "ideal assistant" responses, followed by RLHF or similar preference optimization. They often hire the same annotation vendors, write similar rater guidelines, and generate synthetic training data with each other's frontier models, a kind of informal distillation.

Preference optimization also rewards surface features. Raters tend to prefer answers that look thorough, polished, confident and well organized. Researchers have described a "typicality bias," where people favor familiar-sounding phrasing. Reward models learn these shortcuts, and optimizing hard against them pushes toward the mode of what got rewarded. That's how you get headers, bullet lists, em-dashes, "delve," "it's important to note," tidy summaries and "great question!"

So the same tics reappear across labs because the same pressures act on similar models.

models.label: Gemini Neon
models.answer:
Post-trained chatbots from different labs converge on the same voice because they are shaped by overlapping training signals, annotator ecosystems, and data feedback loops. During reinforcement learning from human feedback, labs use similar alignment rubrics that reward helpfulness, politeness, clarity, and thoroughness, and they often rely on the same global pools of human raters. Under time pressure, annotators consistently favor neatly structured, upbeat, and diplomatically hedged prose, steering independent models toward identical habits like formulaic transitions, emphatic contrasts, and cautious disclaimers.

Optimization itself amplifies this uniformity. Preference-tuning algorithms sharpen a model's output distribution around high-reward phrasing, causing stylistic mode collapse that replaces idiosyncratic voice with safe, reliably rated templates. Finally, cross-pollination cements the shared dialect: labs routinely use frontier models to generate synthetic training data and serve as automated judges, while pretraining corpora increasingly absorb AI-generated web text. Even without sharing code or weights, competing models effectively imitate one another and optimize for the same narrow target of a "good" answer.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Sol
models.answer:
Different labs train their chatbots to succeed at much the same job. Base models already learn many of the same conventions from overlapping kinds of web text. Post-training then makes a narrower register the default. When training examples and preference ratings consistently favor answers that are clear, polite, structured, and cautious, models learn recurring ways to deliver those qualities: acknowledge the question, lay out the answer in tidy sections, add a caveat, and finish with a recap.

Individual tics can ride along with that register. A phrase or punctuation mark can become more frequent simply because it tends to appear in answers that score well. Synthetic training data can reinforce the pattern when one model’s answers become examples for another. Labs can therefore converge on a recognizable house style even with different models and training pipelines.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Astra
models.answer:
Different labs often select for similar answers. Their models learn from overlapping bodies of text, and post-training rewards responses that people or automated judges rate as clear, helpful, and polite. When two answers are equally accurate, the one that looks organized at a glance may win a comparison. Across many comparisons, a small preference can turn into a habit. A model may start adding a tidy recap even when the answer is only a paragraph long.

Imitation can reinforce that convergence. Some labs train on synthetic answers from other models or use other models as judges, so one model’s phrasing can become another’s example of good writing. Similar tics can therefore arise independently or spread between models. A particular phrase alone tells you little about which route it took.
